newsitem.title: GERMANY: German opposition leader slammed for EMU doubts.
newsitem.headline: German opposition leader slammed for EMU doubts.

text.p: One of Germany's leading opposition Social Democrats (SPD) has come under heavy criticism, even within his own party, after calling for a postponement of the European single currency.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Free Democrat (FDP) coalition partners blasted the popular Lower Saxony state premier Gerhard Schroeder on Monday for saying he thought European monetary union (EMU) should not be launched on schedule in January 1999.

"Keeping to the Maastricht criteria is an economic necessity," said Helmut Haussmann, the FDP's European affairs spokesman. "Those who oppose this convergence course want to avoid reforms and flee into a policy of easy money."
Kohl's Finance Minister, Theo Waigel, also called Schroeder irresponsible.

Schroeder, the main rival to SPD chairman Oskar Lafontaine and a possible SPD challenger to Kohl in the 1998 general election, said in an interview with the Bild newspaper "if Germany is not included, the whole thing makes no sense.

"If the government is honest with citizens, then the way things stand today, it must say "no matter how sorry we are, we will not achieve it by the planned date and are delaying the project,'" he said.
Despite such remarks, party colleagues denied the SPD, Bonn's main opposition, had turned against the single currency.
"The goal must be that it happens and that as many European states as possible take part in it," said Hesse state premier Hans Eichel.

The SPD has been keen to shake off negative attitudes toward European integration since the party fell on its face in March with a Euro-sceptical regional election campaign that even many Social Democrats said hinted of right-wing "D-mark nationalism."
